title: Cardiopulmonary and Exercise Physiology (PIO 414/416)
description: Integrated cardiorespiratory responses to exercise, energy systems, training adaptations, environmental physiology and fitness testing.

topics.title: Energy Systems in Exercise
topics.summary: ATP–PCr, glycolytic and oxidative systems, oxygen deficit and EPOC.

notes.b: Muscles use ATP, which is regenerated by three systems. The phosphagen (ATP–phosphocreatine) system provides immediate energy for about 10 seconds of maximal effort (sprints, jumps) via creatine kinase. Anaerobic glycolysis supplies energy for about 10 seconds to 2 minutes of intense effort (400 m sprint), producing lactate and H+ that contribute to fatigue. The oxidative (aerobic) system — carbohydrate and fat oxidation in mitochondria — dominates activities longer than about 2–3 minutes (endurance running) and yields far more ATP per substrate. The crossover concept: as intensity increases, reliance shifts from fat to carbohydrate. The respiratory exchange ratio (RER = VCO2/VO2) is about 0.7 for fat and 1.0 for carbohydrate.

At the start of exercise, oxygen uptake lags behind demand (oxygen deficit), covered by the phosphagen and glycolytic systems. After exercise, oxygen uptake remains elevated — excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC, formerly 'oxygen debt') — to restore PCr and ATP, clear lactate, reload myoglobin and haemoglobin with oxygen, and cope with raised temperature and catecholamines. The lactate threshold is the intensity at which blood lactate begins to rise sharply; it is a strong predictor of endurance performance and improves with training.
k: EPOC restores PCr and clears lactate

topics.title: Cardiovascular Responses to Exercise
topics.summary: Heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, blood pressure and blood flow redistribution during exercise.

notes.b: During dynamic exercise, cardiac output increases from about 5 L/min at rest to 20–25 L/min in untrained and up to 35–40 L/min in elite endurance athletes, through increased heart rate (sympathetic stimulation, vagal withdrawal) and stroke volume (increased venous return via the muscle and respiratory pumps, Frank–Starling mechanism and contractility). Systolic blood pressure rises while diastolic stays similar or falls slightly (vasodilation in muscle), so mean pressure rises modestly. Blood flow is redistributed: working muscle receives up to 80–85% of cardiac output (from about 15–20% at rest), with reduced flow to viscera and kidneys; skin flow increases for thermoregulation. The a–v O2 difference widens as muscles extract more oxygen. Static (isometric) exercise causes a marked rise in both systolic and diastolic pressure.
k: SBP rises; DBP stable or falls
Muscle gets up to 80–85% of CO

notes.b: Oxygen consumption VO2 = cardiac output × arterio-venous O2 difference (Fick principle). VO2max, the maximal rate of oxygen uptake, is the gold-standard measure of cardiorespiratory fitness (about 35–45 mL/kg/min in average young adults; up to 70–85 in elite endurance athletes), limited mainly by maximal cardiac output (central factors) in healthy people. It is expressed in METs: 1 MET ≈ 3.5 mL O2/kg/min (resting oxygen consumption). Maximal heart rate is roughly 220 − age.

topics.title: Respiratory Responses to Exercise
topics.summary: Ventilation during exercise, ventilatory thresholds, gas exchange and limits.

notes.b: Minute ventilation (VE = tidal volume × respiratory rate) rises from about 6 L/min at rest to over 100 L/min at maximal exercise (up to 150–200 L/min in large athletes). At the start of exercise there is an abrupt rise (neural — central command and muscle mechanoreceptors), followed by a slower rise matching metabolic demand. At moderate intensity, tidal volume increases first; at higher intensities, respiratory rate rises more. The ventilatory threshold occurs when VE rises disproportionately to VO2, because buffering of lactic acid by bicarbonate produces extra CO2 (VE/VCO2 later rises too). Arterial PO2 and PCO2 remain close to normal in healthy people except at very high intensities.
k: Ventilatory threshold: extra CO2 from buffering

notes.b: In healthy untrained people, ventilation is not usually the limiting factor for exercise; the cardiovascular system is. In lung disease (COPD, asthma), ventilatory limitation and dynamic hyperinflation limit exercise. Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction occurs in susceptible individuals, especially in cold, dry air — prevented with pre-exercise salbutamol and warm-up. Some elite endurance athletes develop exercise-induced arterial hypoxaemia. Training improves ventilatory muscle endurance and reduces ventilation at a given submaximal workload, but lung volumes change little.
k: Training ↓ submaximal VE; lung volumes change little

topics.title: Training Adaptations
topics.summary: Cardiovascular, muscular and metabolic adaptations to endurance and resistance training.

notes.b: Endurance training increases stroke volume (eccentric left ventricular hypertrophy — the 'athlete's heart'; increased plasma volume), lowering resting and submaximal heart rate (resting bradycardia of 40–60 bpm in athletes is normal); increases maximal cardiac output and VO2max; increases capillary density, mitochondrial number and oxidative enzymes, and myoglobin in muscles; improves fat oxidation (sparing glycogen); raises the lactate threshold; and reduces blood pressure, improves insulin sensitivity and lipid profile (raises HDL).

Resistance training first produces neural adaptations (increased motor unit recruitment and firing rate, better coordination, reduced co-activation of antagonists) within weeks, then muscle hypertrophy (increased cross-sectional area of fibres, particularly type II) over months; it also increases bone mineral density and tendon strength. Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy may occur in strength athletes. Detraining ('reversibility') leads to loss of VO2max and stroke volume within weeks of inactivity; bed rest causes rapid deconditioning (reduced plasma volume, orthostatic intolerance, muscle and bone loss), which is why early mobilisation is important in hospital.

topics.title: Environmental Physiology and Fitness Testing
topics.summary: Exercise in heat, at altitude and in water; heat illness; and fitness assessment.

notes.b: In hot, humid environments (common in Nigeria), heat loss depends on sweating and evaporation; high humidity limits evaporation, raising heat-illness risk. Dehydration reduces plasma volume, stroke volume and performance. Heat illness ranges from heat cramps and heat exhaustion (weakness, heavy sweating, core temperature < 40 °C) to heat stroke (core temperature > 40 °C with CNS dysfunction — confusion, collapse — a medical emergency requiring rapid cooling). Heat acclimatisation over 7–14 days increases plasma volume, sweat rate and earlier sweating, and reduces sweat sodium. At altitude, lower barometric pressure reduces PO2, causing hyperventilation, tachycardia and reduced VO2max; acclimatisation includes increased erythropoietin and red cell mass; acute mountain sickness, high-altitude pulmonary and cerebral oedema are risks.
k: Heat stroke: > 40 °C + CNS dysfunction — cool rapidly

notes.b: Fitness components: cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength and endurance, flexibility, body composition and (skill-related) balance, agility and power. Tests: direct VO2max (treadmill/cycle ergometer with gas analysis), submaximal tests (Åstrand cycle test, step tests), field tests (Cooper 12-minute run, multistage 20 m shuttle 'bleep' test, 6-minute walk test in clinical populations), grip dynamometry and 1RM for strength, sit-and-reach for flexibility, and body composition (BMI, waist circumference, skinfolds, bioelectrical impedance). The Borg scale rates perceived exertion. Pre-participation screening (e.g. PAR-Q) identifies those needing medical clearance.
